attempts.raw_response: Avoid accusatory tones or aggressive questioning, as these often trigger defensiveness rather than honesty. Instead, employ open-ended questions that invite detailed narratives without leading the witness. Phrases like “Can you walk me through what happened?” encourage elaboration, whereas yes-or-no queries shut down dialogue. Maintaining a calm, neutral demeanor helps build rapport, making the subject feel safe enough to share sensitive information. Additionally, active listening demonstrates respect and encourages further disclosure. By focusing on understanding rather than interrogation, you create an environment where truthfulness becomes more likely, allowing subtle inconsistencies to emerge naturally within the flow of conversation rather than through forced confrontation.

pair.human_continuation: Using language that implies fault may cause the person to withhold. Selecting less harsh words can encourage the person to tell the truth. For instance, use the word “took” instead of “stole” or “spent time with someone” rather than “cheated.” The person may be more apt to admit guilt if you use more favorable language. Bluffing is a dangerous, yet often effective, tactic. It involves you making a threat or coming out with what you think is the truth, even though you may not really plan to fulfill the threat or have evidence. Your bluff may tempt the person to tell the truth because they feel like they’ve been exposed or are afraid of the supposed consequences.
pair.prefix: They may also be inconsistent with their answers, which could show they are lying. You could also ask them to tell their story starting from the end and leading up to the beginning or ask them to start in the middle. Relaying the story back may cause them to create errors in their story, which could show they aren’t telling the truth. The language you use can play a huge role in whether a person tells you the truth or not.
